title: What does a ball of functions look like?

prereqs.why: The question is what the definition of an open ball says once the points are functions.
The metric is the supremum one, so the ball is defined by a condition on a supremum.
That a continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains its supremum is what makes one of the four answers exactly right rather than nearly right.

statement:
Work in $\bigl(C[0,1], \|\cdot\|_\infty\bigr)$ and let $f(t) = t$.

The open ball of radius 1 about $f$ is

$$B(f, 1) = \bigl\{\, g \in C[0,1] : \|g - f\|_\infty < 1 \,\bigr\}.$$

Which of the following describes exactly the same set of functions?
hints: Write out $\|g-f\|_\infty < 1$ as a statement about $\sup_t |g(t) - t|$, and then ask what that says about each individual $t$.
A supremum being below 1 certainly implies that every value is below 1. The question is whether the converse holds here.
If $|g(t) - t| < 1$ for every $t \in [0,1]$, is $\sup_t |g(t) - t| < 1$ or only $\le 1$? The domain is a closed bounded interval and $|g - f|$ is continuous, which settles it.

options: The continuous $g$ with $t - 1 < g(t) < t + 1$ for every $t \in [0,1]$.
The continuous $g$ with $t - 1 < g(t) < t + 1$ for at least one $t \in [0,1]$.
The continuous $g$ whose graph lies in the closed strip $t - 1 \le g(t) \le t + 1$.
